subject: Biology
title: Saltwater Chemistry
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Saltwater Chemistry.

hook.text: Seawater contains every naturally occurring element—including gold. About 20 million tons of it.

buildup.text: Ocean salinity averages 3.5%—mostly sodium chloride washed in by rivers over billions of years.

discovery.text: Salt concentration affects density, which drives deep ocean currents that circulate heat globally.

twist.text: The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean—so dense that humans float effortlessly.

climax.text: Marine organisms evolved specialized cells to manage salt balance—a process called osmoregulation.

punchline.text: Gold in every wave. Just not worth mining.

quiz.question: What is the average salinity of ocean water?

details.summary: Seawater contains about 35 grams of dissolved salts per liter, primarily sodium chloride, along with magnesium, sulfate, calcium, and potassium. This chemistry governs ocean density, circulation patterns, and the biological processes of every marine organism from plankton to whales.
details.whyItMatters: Ocean chemistry determines which organisms can survive where and drives global circulation patterns that regulate climate. Human-caused changes to ocean chemistry through acidification and pollution threaten marine ecosystems worldwide.
takeaways: Average ocean salinity is about 35 parts per thousand across all oceans
Salinity differences drive thermohaline circulation and deep water formation
Marine organisms evolved specialized systems to manage salt and water balance

faq.question: Why is the ocean salty?
faq.answer: Rivers carry dissolved minerals from weathering rocks to the sea. Water evaporates but salts remain, concentrating over billions of years. Hydrothermal vents also add dissolved minerals. The composition has remained relatively stable for hundreds of millions of years.

faq.question: How do marine animals cope with salt water?
faq.answer: Fish that live in saltwater constantly lose water through osmosis and must drink seawater, excreting excess salt through specialized gill cells. Sharks maintain internal salt concentrations using urea. Each marine group evolved different osmoregulation strategies.
